catalog_quote: In Ahtna a strong primary stress is placed on the rightmost stem syllable in a word. From my subjective survey of tape-recorded Ahtna stories, it seems that secondary stress is placed equally on other syllables providing that they contain short vowels. ... The syllable receiving the strong stress is easily recognized. In the above examples, the other syllables are either affixes (prefixes such as c'e-, u-, 'es-, da-, ka-, ta-, or suffixes, such as -e', -i, -de, -den, -dze') or incorporated or compound stems that are to the left of another stem (such as tsi- and ts'es-). 'Cottonwood' is a disyllabic root in which the right-most syllable is stressed. However, if a word contains one or more long vowels, (CVV), or a vowel plus the sonorant y (CVy) before the stem syllable, primary stress is placed on each of the long vowels as well as the stem syllable. A pair of words with contrasting stress patterns is: iyaan he is eating it, kiiyaan they are eating it. The word-initial i- in the first word is not as long as the vowel in kii- in the second word, and the second verb seems to have stress equally placed on both syllables.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Ahtena (ahte1237) is not in the catalog. All three title-hit items were obtained and read: Leer 1976 (ANLA scan, scanned) is a comparative tonogenesis paper on Proto-Athabaskan with no stress/accent content and Ahtna only in consonant-reflex notes; Berez 2009 (ANLA draft, scanned) and Berez-Kroeker 2011 (open ScholarSpace copy of the Functions of Language article) are discourse-prosody/intonation-unit studies that only summarize Tuttle's word-stress findings second-hand ('stem syllables are usually the main stress domain of the word'; stressed vowels longer, not pitch-marked). The authoritative first-hand statement remains Kari 1990 Ahtna Athabaskan Dictionary sec. 3.4 (p. 17; App. G sec. 2.18 p. 656; already held by the project): primary stress on the rightmost stem syllable, extra primary stresses on prefixal long vowels (CVV/CVy), no tone; Tuttle 2008 (Linguistics 46, held by the project) confirms acoustically that main stress is morphologically assigned stem stress. Unread: Tuttle 2003 SSILA paper (not found online; results reported in Tuttle 2008) and Tuttle 2009 Upper Ahtna grammar reference (ANLA non-digital) — both low priority. discovery used Glottolog, ANLA's JSON API, Semantic Scholar's API and direct downloads.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No lexical tone; predictable stress. Primary stress falls on the rightmost stem (root) syllable of the word; prefixes, suffixes/enclitics and incorporated/compounded stems to the left of the head stem are unstressed, so the stressed stem may be followed by unstressed suffixes. Additionally any prefixal long vowel (CVV or CVy) preceding the stem also receives a primary stress (e.g. kiiyaan with two stresses vs iyaan with one). In disyllabic roots (t'aghes 'cottonwood') the rightmost syllable is stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Kari (impressionistic): secondary stress 'placed equally on other syllables providing that they contain short vowels'; prefixal long vowels get an additional primary (not secondary) stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Suffixes never carry primary stress; incorporated/compound stems left of another stem are unstressed; word-final h only after a stressed short vowel; minor dialect differences in stress placement arise from gh-/z-/c'-vocalization creating long vowels (sec. 4.6, e.g. CLW diist'as vs Mentasta dezest'as); Tuttle 2008 adds that postpositions and frequent particles are low-stress and that stems are often non-final in verbs and deverbal nouns.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level; Kari states stress location is the key to word division (next primary stress after a stressed stem+suffix belongs to the next word). Examples are citation forms and place names; Tuttle 2008 confirms stem-vowel lengthening in connected narrative speech independent of phrase-final lowering.
new_statements.identity_note: Kari 1990 describes all four Ahtna dialects (Central, Lower, Western, Mentasta/Upper) and states the stress system is uniform across them (sec. 4.6), with minor differences where vocalization rules create prefixal long vowels. Tuttle 2008's instrumental data are from an Upper Ahtna (Mentasta) speaker, Katie John. Glottocode ahte1237 covers all.

new_statements.reading: Ahtna is non-tonal with morphologically assigned stress: primary stress on the rightmost stem syllable (suffixes following the stem are unstressed, so surface position is final or near-final depending on suffixation), plus additional primary stresses on any prefixal long vowel (CVV or CVy). Stress is predictable from morphology, not from a fixed edge count; secondary stress on other short-vowel syllables. Tuttle 2008 (Linguistics 46) confirms acoustically: stem stress = morphological prominence, cued by duration and falling contour, not pitch; Berez 2009/2011 repeat this second-hand. Suitable coding: morphological (stem) stress, non-tonal, with weight-sensitive extra stresses on long prefix vowels.

sources.quote: Some Athabaskan languages, such as Tanacross, Chipewyan, and Navajo, have a tone system in which syllables have a distinctive high or low pitch. Ahtna does not retain this distinction. Instead it has a stress system that follows a regular pattern. Since stress can be predicted, it is not marked in the Ahtna writing system. [...] In Ahtna a strong primary stress is placed on the rightmost stem syllable in a word. From my subjective survey of tape-recorded Ahtna stories, it seems that secondary stress is placed equally on other syllables providing that they contain short vowels. [...] However, if a word contains one or more long vowels, (CVV), or a vowel plus the sonorant y (CVy) before the stem syllable, primary stress is placed on each of the long vowels as well as the stem syllable.
sources.locator: Introduction, sec. 3.4 'Stress', pp. 17-18 (PDF pp. 27-28); see also sec. 4.6 p. 28 and Appendix G sec. 2.18 p. 656
sources.note: Introduction sec. 3.4 'Stress' (pp. 17-18): Ahtna has no tone; predictable stress, unmarked in orthography; strong primary stress on the rightmost stem syllable of the word; prefixal long vowels (CVV, CVy) before the stem also get primary stress; secondary stress 'equally on other syllables' with short vowels; suffixes unstressed; stress marks word boundaries. Sec. 4.6 (p. 28): stress system uniform across dialects, minor differences from vocalization rules. Appendix G 2.18 (p. 656): two rules -- primary stress to rightmost stem, then additional primary stress to prefixal long vowels.

sources.citation: Berez-Kroeker [Berez], Andrea L. (2011). Prosody as a genre-distinguishing feature in Ahtna: a quantitative approach. Functions of Language 18(2): 210-236. DOI 10.1075/fol.18.2.03ber.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 215: "We already have considerable understanding of word-level prosody in Ahtna, which is discussed summarily in Tuttle (2008). ... Spontaneous discourse data has shown that stress and intonation are distinct in Ahtna: while stressed vowels were found to be longer than unstressed vowels, they were not differentiated by higher or lower pitch." p. 221: "Tuttle shows Ahtna stem-initial consonants to be longer than those in prefixes or suffixes, and stem syllables are usually the main stress domain of the word."
sources.locator: sec. 1.3 'Previous work on prosody in Ahtna', p. 215; sec. on confounds, p. 221
sources.note: Discourse-level study (intonation units, pause, pitch reset, boundary tones, syllable pacing) of genre in Ahtna; no first-hand word-stress analysis. Second-hand summary (citing Tuttle 2003, 2008): word stress falls on stem syllables ('stem syllables are usually the main stress domain of the word'); stressed vowels are longer, not higher/lower in pitch; unstressed short vowels reduce to [schwa] (p. 221). Consistent with Kari 1990.

sources.quote: p. 461: "On the basis of these three small studies of Ahtna phonetics, it looks as if morphologically defined prominence — that is, stem stress — is a salient fact for the speakers recorded. This is consistent with Kari's description of the language. Since main stress is morphologically assigned, stem stress and morphological prominence are really the same thing." p. 458: "stressed vowels (segregated for inherent length) are longer than unstressed vowels, and much more likely to carry a falling contour, but they are not higher or lower in pitch than other vowels."

sources.quote: One of the major purposes of this paper is to formulate a hypothesis of the development of tone in modern Athabaskan from an earlier (pre-Proto-Athabaskan) system of vowel nuclei. The impulse to find such an explanation came out of my field-work with the Tongass dialect of Tlingit

sources.note: Comparative-historical paper on tonogenesis (constriction/glottalization of PA vowel nuclei giving high vs. low tone reflexes in Kutchin, Chipewyan, Navajo, Sarcee). The scanned of all 86 scan pages has zero hits for 'stress' or 'accent'. Ahtna appears only in segmental reflex tables (e.g. 'The actual reflexes of final glottalized stops vary within Ahtna.. in upper Ahtna T'> D' stem-finally', scan p. 25). Nothing on Ahtna stress placement.
